texts.0: SP, due to extended head-down time on the navigation log and the GPS page, did not check the surrounding space uninterruptedly and left whole sectors unscanned for the length of a full pattern leg. The outside scan stopped completely while route work was in progress and was not resumed on SP initiative. The IP took control and cleared the turn before SP re-established any lookout.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan pattern that stayed locked on the nose sector, checked the surrounding space only intermittently and omitted the sectors abeam and behind the aircraft. Coverage stayed at the lowest acceptable limit for most of the navigation legs. A continuous scan was restored only after repeated verbal reminders from the IP, without control intervention being required.
texts.2: SP, due to task loading during turning point identification, allowed the outside scan to lapse for a short interval on the crosswind leg and left the rear quadrant unchecked. SP recognized the omission without prompting and restored full sector coverage before initiating the next turn. The lapse stayed short of the limit and had no effect on separation.
texts.3: SP checked the surrounding space uninterruptedly throughout the sortie, sequencing the forward, abeam and rear sectors so that no quadrant was left unchecked. Head-down periods for navigation work were kept short and were each followed by a complete outside sweep. Scan coverage was maintained on every leg of the airport traffic pattern.
texts.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted and systematic outside scan for the entire sortie, fitting cockpit tasks between scan sweeps rather than allowing them to interrupt the lookout. Every turn was cleared through the full arc before it was initiated, including in the traffic pattern where scan rate was highest. Sector coverage was complete and evenly distributed from taxi to shutdown.
texts.marginal: SP checked the surrounding space within standards, but scan coverage was uneven and biased toward the forward sector, with the rear quadrant swept noticeably less often as route work increased. The standard was met on every leg, with the margin narrowing in the busiest navigation segments. SP is expected to distribute scan time evenly across all sectors regardless of cockpit workload.

error_modes.label: Timely detection of traffic and separation action

texts.0: SP, due to a scan that was not sequenced to the geometry of the traffic pattern, did not detect nearby moving aircraft in time and allowed the range to close to a point where a normal avoidance maneuver was no longer available. No separation action was initiated by SP at any stage. The IP took control and maneuvered the aircraft to re-establish separation and prevent a midair conflict.
texts.1: SP, due to a lookout concentrated on the intended track, detected the converging traffic only after the IP called it and reduced separation to the minimum still acceptable. The avoidance turn was made, but late and with an abrupt input rather than an early measured one. No control intervention by the IP was needed once the traffic had been pointed out.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed transition of the scan to the sector where the traffic was developing, acquired the other aircraft later than required and closed inside the separation planned for the leg. SP detected the conflict unaided and initiated an early, smooth turn that restored appropriate separation well before it became critical. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP detected nearby flying aircraft early, called each contact and maintained appropriate separation throughout. Where geometry required it, SP maneuvered in good time and with measured control inputs to keep the situation from developing into a hazard. Traffic in the pattern and along the route was acquired visually before it became a factor.
texts.4: SP acquired every nearby aircraft at long range, called it with position and relative motion, and adjusted track to preserve separation before any conflict geometry could form. Avoidance action, where taken, was anticipatory rather than reactive and cost nothing in navigation accuracy. Detection performance was well ahead of the requirement for this phase of training.
texts.marginal: SP detected nearby aircraft and maintained appropriate separation within standards, but acquisitions came consistently at the later end of the usable range and left less time than desirable for a measured response. The trend was most evident on the legs with the highest cockpit workload. SP is expected to move detection earlier so that separation is preserved by track adjustment rather than by a corrective turn.

texts.0: SP, due to a loss of situational awareness after falling behind the route plan, stopped monitoring the R/T effectively and missed the position reports of the traffic sharing the working area and the pattern. No mental picture of the surrounding traffic was built at any point on the leg. The IP had to take over the radio picture and direct the aircraft clear of the reported traffic.
texts.1: SP, due to a loss of situational awareness while reconstructing position over the route, monitored the R/T only in fragments and missed calls that were relevant to the airspace being flown. The traffic picture reached the minimum acceptable level only after the IP repeated the missed calls verbally. SP flew the aircraft correctly, but the awareness was borrowed rather than built.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the turning point identification, missed a position report from traffic entering the same sector and briefly held an incomplete picture of the airspace. SP identified the gap unprompted, requested a repeat on the frequency and rebuilt the traffic picture before the conflict geometry could develop. Awareness was restored without any intervention.
texts.3: SP monitored the R/T effectively and continuously, using the reported positions to build situational awareness and to anticipate where conflicting traffic would appear. Calls relevant to the route and to the pattern were interpreted correctly and translated into an outside scan of the appropriate sector. No airborne threat developed without SP being aware of it first.
texts.4: SP monitored the frequency continuously and converted the radio picture into a precise, running model of who was where, using it to pre-position the visual scan before each contact became visible. Traffic entering the working area was anticipated from its first call and cleared visually without delay. Radio-derived awareness was complete and consistently ahead of events.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the R/T and built an adequate traffic picture within standards, but the picture thinned whenever navigation workload peaked and had to be reconstructed afterwards from later calls. Awareness stayed acceptable on every leg, with the margin at its narrowest around the turning points. SP is expected to sustain continuous R/T monitoring so that the traffic picture is maintained rather than rebuilt.

texts.0: SP, due to holding the planned track and altitude without assessing the developing cloud along the route, did not maintain appropriate VFR distance from clouds and flew into a position from which the visual references and the lookout were lost. No deviation or descent was initiated to preserve VMC. The IP took control and repositioned the aircraft clear of cloud.
texts.1: SP, due to a late assessment of the cloud base ahead, closed to a distance from cloud that left only the minimum acceptable VFR margin and reduced the useful field of view for clearing. SP deviated only after the IP verbally directed a heading and altitude change. The aircraft remained VFR, but the correction was reactive and late.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow read of the cloud development ahead on the leg, allowed the distance from cloud to reduce below what had been planned for the route. SP recognized the trend without prompting and offset the track early, restoring a comfortable VFR margin well before the standard was at risk. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained appropriate VFR distance from clouds throughout the route, adjusting track and altitude in good time as the cloud pattern changed. The lookout arc was never restricted by proximity to cloud on any leg. Deviations for weather were planned ahead and cost nothing in navigation accuracy.
texts.4: SP read the cloud development well ahead of the aircraft and routed around it early, holding a generous VFR margin at every point without any late or abrupt correction. Clearing coverage was preserved unrestricted throughout, and the deviations were flown back onto track with the plan intact. Weather management supported the lookout instead of competing with it.
texts.marginal: SP maintained VFR distance from clouds within standards, but the margins were repeatedly taken up before a deviation was flown and were smaller than the conditions warranted. Standards were met on every leg, with the closest margins occurring where the cloud was building fastest. SP is expected to assess the cloud pattern earlier and build the offset before the margin has to be defended.

error_modes.label: Attention allocation inside versus outside the cockpit

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck created by a single unresolved GPS indication, allocated essentially all attention inside the cockpit and abandoned both the visual and the verbal clearing task. Aircraft control degraded at the same time, with heading and altitude left unattended while the indication was being worked. The IP took control to restore the flight path and the lookout.
texts.1: SP, due to an attention bottleneck around one navigation discrepancy, allocated attention heavily inside the cockpit and left the outside and R/T clearing at the minimum acceptable level. Aircraft control was retained but the division of attention was restored only after the IP verbally directed SP to look out and fly the aircraft. The correction came late in the leg.
texts.2: SP, due to attention being captured briefly by an unexpected cockpit indication, let the balance between inside and outside work shift and reduced the clearing effort for a short period. SP recognized the imbalance unprompted, set the indication aside and returned to a correct division of attention between visual scan, R/T and aircraft control. Control of the aircraft was never in question.
texts.3: SP allocated attention correctly between work inside and outside the cockpit, taking in the visual and verbal cues needed to avoid a midair conflict or a CFIT situation while keeping the aircraft under control. Navigation tasks were broken into short segments that never displaced the clearing task. The division of attention held through the busiest phases of the route.
texts.4: SP divided attention between cockpit work and the outside picture with no observable cost to either, interleaving navigation tasks, R/T and the visual scan so that all three ran continuously. Unexpected indications were parked and handled at the next low-workload point rather than absorbing the scan. Aircraft control remained precise throughout.
texts.marginal: SP allocated attention between inside and outside work within standards, but the balance shifted inward whenever a navigation task did not resolve immediately, and the outside picture thinned for those periods. Standards were met on every leg, with the least margin around the turning points and the GPS work. SP is expected to cap the time spent on any single cockpit task so the clearing effort stays constant.

error_modes.label: Clearing as Leader - hazard recognition and clearing technique

texts.0: SP, while in charge of the formation and due to a lookout that was not extended to the sectors into which the formation was turning, did not conceive the developing hazard and did not regulate the flight parameters to avoid it. Admissible clearing techniques were not applied before the turns, leaving the wingman's side unchecked. The IP took control of the lead aircraft to clear the formation from the conflict.
texts.1: SP, while leading, checked the airspace only intermittently and located the nearby aircraft late, allowing the formation to close to the minimum acceptable separation. The heading and altitude adjustment needed to avoid the traffic was made only after the IP verbally directed it. Clearing technique before the turns was applied, but incompletely and behind events.
texts.2: SP, while leading and due to attention held on the navigation plan, was slow to recognize a developing conflict with traffic in the working area. SP identified the hazard unaided and regulated heading and altitude early enough to open the separation before it became a factor for the formation. Clearing technique before subsequent turns was applied correctly without prompting.
texts.3: SP checked the airspace continuously for the whole period in charge of the formation, including in the landing pattern, and located nearby aircraft in time to keep proper separation for both aircraft. Active and potential hazards were recognized and the flight parameters were regulated in good time to avoid them. Admissible clearing techniques were applied before every turn.
texts.4: SP led with a clearing effort that covered the full arc into which the formation was maneuvering, acquiring traffic early and adjusting the formation flight path before any conflict geometry could form. Clearing technique before each turn was complete and unhurried, and the wingman was never placed in an unclear sector. Separation management in the landing pattern was of check-ride standard.
texts.marginal: SP checked the airspace and maintained proper separation for the formation within standards, but hazard recognition came late enough that the avoiding adjustments were larger than they needed to be. The standard was met throughout the period in charge, with the margin narrowest in the landing pattern. SP is expected to clear further ahead into the turn so that flight parameters can be regulated in small, early increments.

texts.0: SP, due to an unagreed division of lookout responsibility within the formation, did not execute clearing appropriate to the No2 position and did not clear towards the Leader while in fingertip. The sector that only the wingman could cover was left unchecked for the whole leg, and no support was provided to No1. The IP intervened to restore the lookout and re-establish the formation's coverage.
texts.1: SP, due to an uncoordinated split of lookout duties with the lead aircraft, executed clearing that was not matched to the relative position in the formation and covered the Leader's side only intermittently in fingertip. Coverage reached the minimum acceptable level after the IP verbally directed where to look. Support to No1 was present but late and incomplete.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the fingertip position references, was slow to extend the lookout towards the Leader and briefly left that sector uncovered. SP recognized the gap unprompted and resumed clearing appropriate to the No2 position, supporting No1 for the remainder of the leg. No prompting or intervention was needed after the initial lapse.
texts.3: SP executed clearing according to the relative position within the formation and cleared towards the Leader throughout fingertip, supporting No1 while recognizing that the main responsibility remained with the lead aircraft. Traffic in the sector covered by the wingman was called in good time. Formation position was maintained while the lookout was carried out.
texts.4: SP cleared the wingman's sector continuously and to the full extent of the position, calling traffic to the Leader early and with an accurate relative description. Lookout towards the Leader in fingertip was sustained without any degradation of formation position. The support provided to No1 measurably improved the formation's overall coverage.
texts.marginal: SP executed position-dependent clearing within standards, but coverage towards the Leader in fingertip thinned whenever formation position required larger corrections. The standard was met on every leg, with the narrowest margin during the closest fingertip work. SP is expected to hold the wingman's lookout at a constant level so that the formation's coverage does not depend on how much position correction is being flown.

error_modes.label: Use of R/T to create safe separation from traffic

texts.0: SP, due to a position report that was neither made nor updated as the route was flown, did not use the R/T to create safe separation from the surrounding air traffic and left other aircraft without any knowledge of the flight's position or intentions. Calls that would have deconflicted the working area and the pattern entry were omitted entirely. The IP made the required transmissions and directed the aircraft clear of the traffic.
texts.1: SP, due to transmissions being deferred until the aircraft was already established on the leg, used the R/T for separation only at the minimum acceptable level, with position reports that were late and lacked intentions. The missing calls were made only after the IP prompted each one verbally. Separation was preserved, but by the other traffic rather than by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to workload around the turning point, made the position report later than planned and initially omitted the intended routing. SP identified the omission unaided and transmitted a complete, accurate report with intentions in time for the surrounding traffic to deconflict. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP used the R/T effectively to create safe separation from the air traffic, transmitting accurate and timely position reports with intentions at the planned points along the route and on pattern entry. Calls were phrased clearly and matched what the aircraft actually did. Other traffic was able to deconflict from SP's transmissions without further coordination.
texts.4: SP used the R/T as an active separation tool, transmitting complete position and intentions ahead of each point where a conflict could form and coordinating directly with the traffic sharing the area. Every call was concise, standard and precisely timed to the phase of flight. Radio work removed potential conflicts before they required any maneuvering.
texts.marginal: SP used the R/T to create separation within standards, but position reports were consistently at the late end of the useful window and intentions were sometimes stated only when questioned. The standard was met at every reporting point, with the least margin on the busiest frequency segments. SP is expected to transmit position and intentions earlier so that separation is established by the call rather than confirmed after it.

error_modes.label: Visual scanning technique - 20-30 degree arcs with a 3-5 second focus point

texts.0: SP, due to a lookout flown as one continuous sweep of the horizon instead of a search of successive arcs of approximately 20-30 degrees, never held the eyes on any single arc long enough for a target to be resolved. No distant point was used inside the arcs, so the scan produced no usable picture of the surrounding airspace and no aircraft was acquired visually during the whole route segment. The IP took control and cleared the sector before the next turn could be flown.
texts.1: SP searched in arcs that were far wider than the 20-30 degrees taught and dwelt on each for well under the 3-5 seconds required to focus on a distant point. Detection ranges stayed at the lowest acceptable limit and traffic was acquired only when it was already close abeam. The scan was broken down into proper arcs and dwell times only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to the pace of the route work, compressed the scan into fast sweeps with a dwell time noticeably short of 3-5 seconds over one navigation leg. SP recognized that no distant focus point was being used, slowed the scan back to arcs of approximately 20-30 degrees and re-established normal detection ranges before the next turning point. The technique lapse stayed short of the limit and no separation issue developed.
texts.3: SP searched the airspace in successive arcs of approximately 20-30 degrees, focusing on a distant point such as a cloud or a ground reference within each arc for 3-5 seconds. The scan was sequenced so that the arcs overlapped and no sector was passed over without a focused look. Traffic was consistently acquired at ranges that left a normal avoidance option available.
texts.4: SP applied the arc-by-arc scanning technique precisely throughout the sortie, holding approximately 20-30 degrees per arc with a firm 3-5 second focus on a distant point and no sector left unsearched. The scan rate was adapted to the traffic density of the route and the pattern without ever degenerating into an unfocused sweep. Every visual acquisition was made at long range and reported before it became a factor.
texts.marginal: SP searched in arcs and used distant focus points within standards, but the dwell time drifted towards the low end of 3-5 seconds and the arcs widened as the navigation workload increased. The technique remained acceptable on every leg, with the margin narrowest between turning points where chart work was heaviest. SP is expected to hold arc width and focus time constant regardless of the cockpit task in progress.

error_modes.label: Refocusing outside after an instrument crosscheck

texts.0: SP, after each crosscheck of the instruments, looked back outside without refocusing on a distant point, leaving the eyes at the natural resting focus of about 18 inches. The lookout was therefore nominally being flown while nothing beyond the canopy was actually being resolved, and traffic in clear air went undetected throughout the leg. The IP took control and manoeuvred clear of an aircraft that had remained unseen by SP.
texts.1: SP returned outside after instrument crosschecks with the eyes still set close to the cockpit focus distance and reacquired distant objects only slowly. Detection of nearby aircraft came at the lowest acceptable limit, after the traffic had already grown large in the canopy. SP began deliberately refocusing on a distant reference only after the IP verbally pointed out the omission, with no control intervention required.
texts.2: SP, due to a heavy instrument and GPS crosscheck at a turning point, transitioned outside once without refocusing on a distant point and searched an empty sky at close focus for a few seconds. SP recognized the effect unprompted, deliberately picked up a distant cloud to reset the focus and restored normal detection ranges before the next leg. No separation issue arose from the lapse.
texts.3: SP refocused on a distant point every time attention returned outside after an instrument crosscheck, countering the eye's natural focus at about 18 inches. Transitions between the cockpit and the outside picture were made deliberately, so that scanning always resumed with the eyes correctly set for distance. Traffic was detected at normal ranges throughout the route and the pattern.
texts.4: SP made every inside-to-outside transition through a deliberate refocus on a distant reference, so that no portion of the scan was flown at cockpit focus distance. The habit was applied consistently after navigation log work, GPS checks and systems crosschecks alike, with no loss of detection range at any stage. Visual acquisition remained uniformly long-range from departure to recovery.
texts.marginal: SP refocused outside after instrument crosschecks within standards, but the refocus was sometimes delayed by a second or two and the first look outside was made at close focus. The technique held on every leg, with the margin narrowing as head-down navigation work increased. SP is expected to make the distant refocus an explicit part of each transition back to the outside scan.

error_modes.label: Detecting an aircraft on a collision course - creating relative movement

texts.0: SP, faced with traffic that stayed on a constant relative bearing and therefore appeared stationary in the canopy, did not use slight heading changes to create the relative movement needed to detect it and did not act on the traffic alert passed by ATC. No wing flash or rock was used although the aircraft was known to be close and had not been visually acquired. The IP took control and manoeuvred to guarantee the flight path was well clear.
texts.1: SP recognized only late that the reported traffic was holding a constant relative bearing and made the slight heading change needed to generate relative movement at the lowest acceptable limit. Visual acquisition came only after the aircraft had grown noticeably in the canopy. The heading change and the subsequent lookout into that quadrant were prompted verbally by the IP rather than initiated by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to the difficulty of picking up an aircraft that appeared stationary against the ground background, searched the reported quadrant for some time without result before recalling the technique. SP then applied a slight heading change unprompted, generated the relative movement required and acquired the traffic in good time to keep the flight path well clear. The delay stayed short of the limit and no avoidance manoeuvre was needed.
texts.3: SP treated traffic that appeared stationary in the canopy as a collision-course indication and used slight heading changes to create the relative movement required for detection. Where the aircraft was known to be close but not yet acquired, a wing flash was used to make the flight visible to the other pilot. Visual acquisition was achieved in time to keep the intended flight path well clear of the other aircraft.
texts.4: SP applied the constant-relative-bearing check continuously along the route and used small heading changes early, so that reported traffic was resolved against the background well before it became a factor. A wing flash or rock was used at once whenever another aircraft was known to be close but not visually acquired. Flight path clearance from every acquired aircraft was maintained with a wide margin and without abrupt manoeuvring.
texts.marginal: SP used heading changes to generate relative movement within standards, but the technique was applied only after a fairly long unsuccessful search of the reported quadrant. Acquisition was achieved on every occasion, with the margin narrowest for traffic converging from the forward quadrants. SP is expected to apply the heading change as soon as a target is suspected of holding a constant bearing rather than after the search has failed.

error_modes.label: Canopy bow masking and clearing turns for the blind spots

texts.0: SP, due to a head position held fixed against the canopy bows, left the sectors masked by the structure permanently unsearched and never used clearing turns to look into the blind areas beneath the fuselage and the wings. Whole quadrants of the working area were therefore never cleared before manoeuvring was initiated. The IP took control and flew the clearing turn required to establish that the area below and behind was clear.
texts.1: SP made only token head movement around the canopy bows and cleared the areas beneath the fuselage and wings at the lowest acceptable limit before manoeuvring in the training area. Clearing turns were flown with shallow bank and well short of approximately 90 degrees off the established heading, so the masked sectors were only partly exposed. The technique was corrected only after verbal direction from the IP, without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the route timing, initiated one manoeuvre in the working area without first clearing the blind area under the nose. SP recognized the omission unprompted, flew a clearing turn with adequate bank to expose the masked sector and confirmed it was clear before continuing. The lapse stayed short of the limit and no conflict developed.
texts.3: SP accounted for the restrictions to visibility created by the canopy bows, moving the head to search the sectors they mask rather than accepting them as unviewable. Clearing turns were used when warranted to clear the blind spots beneath the fuselage and the wings, particularly in the training areas. Each turn used enough bank, up to approximately 90 degrees off the established heading, to expose the area being cleared.
texts.4: SP searched around the canopy bows continuously with deliberate head movement, treating the masked sectors as areas requiring more attention rather than less. Clearing turns were flown before every manoeuvre in the training area, with high enough bank and sufficient heading change to expose the full area beneath the fuselage and wings. No portion of the surrounding airspace was left unsearched at any point of the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP cleared around the canopy bows and beneath the aircraft within standards, but the head movement was limited and the clearing turns used less bank than needed to fully expose the lower blind spots. The requirement was met before every manoeuvre, with the margin narrowest in the training area. SP is expected to increase both head movement and clearing turn bank so that the masked sectors are searched as thoroughly as the open ones.

error_modes.label: Reliance on ATC separation and radar monitoring instead of see-and-avoid

texts.0: SP, on the assumption that radar monitoring, the assigned flying area and ATC separation removed the need to look out, effectively suspended visual clearing for the whole leg. These aids assist in but do not relieve the pilot of the responsibility to clear, and SP had no visual picture of the traffic actually sharing the airspace. The IP took control and manoeuvred clear of an aircraft that neither ATC nor SP had called.
texts.1: SP treated the assigned area and the radar service as the primary means of separation and used the outside scan only as a secondary check, keeping visual clearing at the lowest acceptable limit. When a traffic call was received SP channelized on the reported position instead of prioritizing the search, although the accuracy of such information varies with conditions and capabilities. Full visual clearing was restored only after repeated verbal direction from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to confidence in the radar service covering the working area, allowed the outside scan to thin out for a short period after being told the area was clear. SP recognized unprompted that the service assists in but does not relieve the responsibility to clear, restored a full scan and acquired the nearby traffic visually in good time. The lapse stayed short of the limit and separation was never in question.
texts.3: SP used radar monitoring, the assigned flying area and ATC separation as aids while retaining visual detection as the primary means of collision avoidance. Traffic information received was translated into a focused search of the correct quadrant rather than accepted as a complete picture. Clearing responsibility was exercised continuously regardless of the services being provided.
texts.4: SP maintained full see-and-avoid responsibility throughout, using the radar service and the area assignment purely to narrow the visual search rather than to replace it. Every traffic call was cross-checked visually and the reported information was weighed against what was actually seen. No period of the sortie relied on an external agency for separation.
texts.marginal: SP kept visual clearing as the primary means of separation within standards, but the scan visibly relaxed on legs where a radar service was being received. The responsibility was met throughout, with the margin narrowest inside the assigned working area. SP is expected to keep the lookout at the same intensity whether or not radar monitoring or ATC separation is available.

error_modes.label: Clearing priority on the low level route - heads up and eyes out
error_modes.source: technique:8.19.6.d ROUTE BASICS - MISSION ELEMENT PRIORITIES

texts.0: SP, due to chart work carried out down in the cockpit instead of with the chart brought up to eye level, spent far less than eighty percent of the low level segment heads up and eyes out. Clearing was displaced by navigation rather than kept as the highest priority task, and terrain clearance was not the focus during the turns, where the greater part of the low level hazard lies. The IP took control to restore terrain and traffic clearance on the route.
texts.1: SP kept the outside picture at the lowest acceptable limit on the low level segment, with head-down chart reading long enough that heads-up time fell to the minimum tolerable. Focus returned to clearing only when prompted, and terrain clearance during the turns was maintained without margin to spare. The chart was raised to eye level and the priorities reordered only after verbal direction from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to an identification problem at a checkpoint, read the chart low in the cockpit for one segment and let heads-up time drop below the intended eighty percent. SP recognized the drift unprompted, raised the chart to eye level and returned the focus to clearing outside before entering the next turn. The deviation stayed short of the limit and terrain and traffic clearance were never compromised.
texts.3: SP kept clearing as the highest priority task on the route, spending about eighty percent of the low level time heads up and eyes out. The chart was brought up to eye level to be read, so that the outside picture was retained while navigating, and the focus was always returned to clearing outside. Terrain clearance was given particular attention during the turns.
texts.4: SP integrated the mission elements in the correct priority order throughout the low level, with clearing consistently first and navigation tasks fitted around it. The chart was always read at eye level and no cockpit task pulled the eyes down for more than a brief interval. Terrain clearance during the turns was managed with a deliberate margin and the route was flown with the outside picture never lost.
texts.marginal: SP kept clearing as the priority task and the chart at eye level within standards, but heads-up time slipped towards the minimum on the busier route segments. The priorities held on every leg, with the margin narrowest in the turns where terrain clearance also demanded attention. SP is expected to plan chart work so that the eighty percent heads-up allocation is preserved even in the most demanding segments.

error_modes.label: Hazard call from the pilot not flying and 500 feet flight path clearance

texts.0: SP, while not flying the aircraft, saw the developing hazard but did not point it out immediately to the pilot flying and passed no clock position, elevation or direction of tracking. With collision becoming imminent SP neither took control nor ensured the intended flight path was well clear of the other aircraft. The IP took control and manoeuvred to restore the 500 feet minimum clearance from the conflicting traffic.
texts.1: SP passed the hazard to the pilot flying at the lowest acceptable limit, with a call that lacked the clock position and the tracking information needed to make the traffic findable. The flight path was adjusted late and the resulting clearance was only just adequate. A complete traffic call in the standard format was made only after the IP directed it verbally, with no control intervention required.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation over whether the contact was a factor, delayed the traffic call to the pilot flying by a few seconds. SP then made a complete call giving clock position, elevation and tracking without prompting and the flight path was adjusted early enough to stay well clear of the other aircraft. The delay stayed short of the limit and the 500 feet minimum was never approached.
texts.3: SP pointed out every hazard immediately to the pilot flying, using the standard format of clock position, elevation and direction of tracking. Where the geometry required it, SP was ready to take control and ensured the intended flight path stayed well clear of the other aircraft by at least 500 feet. Crew coordination on traffic was clear and unambiguous throughout.
texts.4: SP called every contact to the pilot flying as soon as it was acquired, with an accurate clock position, elevation and tracking that allowed immediate acquisition by the other cockpit. Flight path adjustments were agreed and made early, keeping clearance from other aircraft far in excess of the 500 feet minimum. The division of duties between pilot flying and pilot not flying was maintained without confusion at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP passed hazard calls to the pilot flying within standards, but some calls omitted the tracking element and were made a little later than the acquisition allowed. Clearance from other aircraft was maintained above the 500 feet minimum throughout, with the margin narrowest for converging traffic in the pattern. SP is expected to call each contact in the complete standard format at the moment it is seen.

error_modes.label: Lost sight of the other aircraft - blind call and altitude separation

texts.0: SP lost sight of the other aircraft and made no blind call at all, leaving the flight without the current altitude needed to deconflict and continuing to manoeuvre towards the last known position. A sun-blind condition earlier in the sortie was likewise treated as a transient nuisance rather than as an actual lost-sight case. The IP took control, transmitted the blind call and established the altitude separation required for deconfliction.
texts.1: SP called blind at the lowest acceptable limit, several seconds after visual contact was lost and without including the current altitude in the transmission. No manoeuvre away from the last known position was initiated while the call went unacknowledged. The complete blind call and the deconflicting manoeuvre were made only after the IP directed them verbally, with no control intervention required.
texts.2: SP, due to a momentary sun-blind condition during a turn, hesitated briefly over whether visual contact had genuinely been lost. SP then treated it correctly as an actual lost-sight case, transmitted the blind call with current altitude unprompted and held a safe flight path until the other aircraft was regained. The delay stayed short of the limit and deconfliction was never in doubt.
texts.3: SP called blind immediately on losing visual contact, stating call sign and current altitude, and manoeuvred away from the last known position when the call was not acknowledged in a timely manner. Where both aircraft were blind, the minimum 1000 feet of altitude separation directed was established and held until visual contact was regained. Relative position information was transmitted or acted upon correctly to rebuild the visual.
texts.4: SP transmitted the blind call the instant visual contact was lost, complete with altitude and the turn or heading in progress, and took positive action to guarantee flight path deconfliction. The 1000 feet altitude separation was established without delay whenever both aircraft were blind, and no rejoin was attempted closer than route position until visual was called. Every sun-blind moment was handled at once as an actual lost-sight case.
texts.marginal: SP made blind calls with altitude and achieved deconfliction within standards, but the calls came a little after the loss of visual and the altitude separation was established slowly. The procedure was completed correctly on each occasion, with the margin narrowest during turns into the sun. SP is expected to transmit the blind call as an immediate reflex and to open altitude separation without waiting for the picture to clarify.
